project.title: Lightweight URL-Based Phishing Detection for Real-Time Browser Use

research.concept: Detect phishing websites from URL lexical features fast enough to run inside a browser.
research.problemStatement: Accurate ML phishing detectors are often too heavy to run in real time inside a browser, leaving a gap between accuracy and efficiency.
research.hypothesis: A Random Forest using only URL lexical features achieves F1 within 2 points of a heavier CNN baseline while using at least 50% less inference compute.

researchQuestions.text: Can URL lexical features alone match a heavier model's F1 on a public phishing dataset?
What is the inference-time cost difference between the lightweight and heavy models?

objectives: Assemble a reproducible URL lexical feature set.
Compare a lightweight model against a classic and a recent baseline on the same split.
Measure accuracy and inference cost together.

contributions.text: A lightweight URL lexical feature set achieving comparable F1 with substantially less inference compute.
An empirical accuracy-vs-efficiency comparison on a public dataset under one fixed split.

researchGap.statement: Existing accurate detectors are too heavy for real-time browser use; the accuracy-vs-efficiency trade-off for URL-only features is under-measured.

inclusionCriteria: reports F1 on a public dataset

sources.title: Machine Learning Approaches to Phishing Detection (synthetic)
Rule-Based Phishing Filters: Strengths and Limits (synthetic)
Choosing Metrics for Imbalanced Security Data (synthetic)

implementation.runtimeNotes: Must run on a laptop CPU.

figures.purpose: Show the detection pipeline from URL to label.
figures.supportsClaim: The method is simple and deployable.

figures.purpose: Plot F1 against inference cost for all models.
figures.supportsClaim: Lightweight model trades little F1 for large cost savings.

limitations: Single public dataset; results may not generalize to all phishing campaigns.
openDecisions: Whether to add a second dataset before submission.
